Question: What is the Official language of Bihar?
Answer: The Official Language of Bihar is Hindi. Bihar was the first Indian state to institutionalize Hindi as state official language in 1881(when it replaced Urdu). The History of Urdu is thus even longer in Bihar. This is the reason Hindi and Urdu are today the first and second official languages of Bihar. The Native spoken Languages are Bhojpuri, Maithili, Magahi, etc but they are not taught in Schools or used in official documents. The associated historical native scripts are also pretty much extinct as Devanagari is the official script. Not only Hindi, but Sanskrit also has good standing in Bihar(usually, that is the 3rd Language in Schools). In our CBSE school located in adjacent Northern Bengal, all Hindi and Sanskrit teachers were either from Bihar or trained there and all had great Pedigree in these Languages. My Younger brother had a Bengali classmate and we were family friends with them. Their mother was also a teacher and had MA/higher studies in Hindi from Bihar. Our Teachers(Singh Sir, Chaudhary Sir, Jha Sir) taught us Shudh Hindi so well that I still haven’t forgotten it.

Question: How similar are Spanish and Portuguese? Are they mutually intelligible?
Answer: Even though I dont know either language but I can share a interaction which I recently saw/heard between a Spanish and Portuguese speaker here in USA. At the Irvine Amtrak Train station sometimes we see International visitors who dont know English at all. So I was at the waiting room, waiting for my Train, when I heard the Security Officer say ‘What Language do you speak?’ , and the answer was ‘Portuguese’ (with the understanding that the visitor cant understand English). That is when I started paying attention. The Security officer started speaking some English, then moved to full Spanish. Or then would start with Spanish and speak some English. The visitor would speak Portuguese with some English/Math terms. (they were talking about Train and Times). Finally, they figured it out. And in the End I heard the Security Officer appologize that She could not speak to the Visitor in her Language. They said greetings to each other and moved on. So, overall from what I saw, It was not a comfortable conversation as far as understading each other, and much of what was interacted/interpreted would have been accomplished by just sign language or hand gestures or pointing at Train Brochure. (well may be it was bit better than that). (From my memory, I remember having such converstations with Japanese, Kazakh, Gujarati or Spanish speaking people who couldnt speak/understand much English). Thus, from my small sample size and understanding, I would say that Spanish and Portuguese are not really mutually intelligible. The people who find more similarities in Languages from same lingusitic family actually have already taken time and interest in learning some words/vocabulary of the other Language. That may cloud their judgement onto how even languages with high lexical similarties can sound pretty different, especially if there is no previous exposure.

Question: Why did the Punjabi language lose its significance in the Punjab province?
Answer: We can make an approximate chronological pattern of ‘Prominent Languages’ of Empires which have ruled over the Punjab region across the Last millennia. Ghaznavid dynasty : 977–1186 , Persian (official and court language; lingua franca) , Arabic (theology), Turkic (military) Ghurid dynasty before 786–1215 , Persian (court, literature) Malmuk Dynasty, 1206–1290, Turkic (main) , Persian (administration) Delhi Sultanate , 1206–1526, Persian (official and court language), Hindavi (semi-official between 1451 and 1526) Mughal Empire, 1526–1857, Persian (official and court language), Urdu (later given official status), Hindustani (lingua franca), Chagatai (spoken in the initial years), Arabic (for religious ceremonies) Sikh Empire , 1799–1849 , Court language (Persian), Spoken languages (Punjabi, Saraiki, Hindko, Pothwari - Pahari, Kangri, Dogri). British Punjab/India, 1849–1947, Urdu (Official Language). West Punjab(Pakistan) has continued with Urdu as it’s official Language. Erstwhile Eastern Punjab(Political) has parts which have Hindi and Punjabi as official Languages. If we analyze this trend, we can see that Punjabi never really had a royal patronage for much of its history. So, Punjabi can’t be compared to Languages like Tamil Or Kannada, or even Urdu/Hindi in that respect. (Dogri/Dogra Akkhar did have Royal Patronage in the hilly regions for a period). But thing is that until 100 or so years ago, this didn’t really harm the language that much. Infact, both Persian and Punjabi thrived in the region for almost 1000 years as mentioned in the following article. The reason for this was that the literacy level was way low during those times, so only the elites would learn Persian or later Urdu. So, Punjabi continued as a famous language of prose and daily use during those times. But over the last 100–150 years, when literacy rates and general mass media consumption started going up, Punjabi or other Languages of the region missed the opportunity to position themselves as a viable languages of governance. This is where the real decline of these Languages started in earnest. (Currently, the erosion is more in Urban regions but over generations it will decline in rural regions too). Still, considering the background of Punjab history, the emergence of Gurmukhi Punjabi can be seen as a success. (half dozen or more ‘Native’ scripts of the region have gone extinct). In this respect, Punjab is different from Bengal, which though also divided over Religion, was still able to maintain and secure its common native Language and Script.

Question: Is Punjabi a dialect of Saraiki/Multani?
Answer: They are languages of a shared region. It is said that the language we call Punjabi today was called Multani at some point. A Landa-based Brahmi script also existed to write Multani called Multani Script[1], belonging to the same family as Gurmukhi but it is extinct today. The first person (Baba Farid) who conferred or helped to give an Independent linguistic identity to the Punjabi Language was from Multan. I also recently saw a video of a Jatki Language speaker claiming that theirs is the real language or ‘sound’ of the Greater Punjab Region. Jatki is closer to Saraiki. Personally, I consider myself an Eastern Punjabi speaker.[2]We have some dialects here also but since the education and mass media is in a Standard form of Punjabi, the dialects will eventually phase out as usually happens. We also generally use the Gurmukhi script. So, I consider Saraiki a separate language. As mentioned there were historical links but there has been divergence along the way. I mean Eastern Punjab is already separated from Western Punjab, so we don't even have any reaction to Southern West Punjab or Saraiki movement, in fact all that already happened on the Eastern side in the 1950–60s with the reorganization of the current Indian Punjab. In the long history of languages, these things happen. Saraiki alphabet is still being developed based on Arabic Sindhi as it shares some sounds with Sindhi and the people of the Lower West Punjab region use Urdu officially and most people who moved to India from that region use Hindi as their language of education. (in regions like Haryana and Delhi). One time I interacted with a Sindhi from Upper Sindh who could speak Saraiki. I also tried to learn the ڳ (ģāf) sound which is little different from Eastern Punjabi. We use Gurmukhi to write Punjabi and use it as an official/literary Language(basically we were able to ‘secure’ the future of the language). I hope Saraiki People can also one day fully develop their Arabic-based Rasm-Ul-Khat like Sindhi and use Saraiki as a Official Language.

Question: Why are Bollywood movies often set in a Punjabi environment?
Answer: The Language of communication of Bollywood is Hindustani (Urdu-Hindi). That means usually one needs good hold or atleast interest in Hindi-Urdu to succeed in Bollywood. Urdu/Hindustani has a history in Punjab going back to 1850’s. Urdu was the official Language of United Punjab till 1947 and continues to be famous/official language in various parts of Northern West India.(as Hindi). It’s said that before Partition, Lahore also had a thriving media industry. Urdu was already becoming prevalent there as it continues today also in Pakistan. Post Partition many Punjabis came to Eastern(Indian) side of Punjab and then later to metros like Delhi/Mumbai etc. For example, Yash Chopra first came to East Punjab (studied in Doaba Khalsa College, Jalandhar but eventually left for Mumbai). One time Yash Chopra was asked when will he make a movie in Punjabi Language, he said that while the backdrop of his movies is Punjabi Culture wise but the Language is Hindustani for larger/wider reach. (This actually is the answer to the question!) From my knowledge he never made a movie in Punjabi Language. Actually, setting in Punjab background (using Hindi-Urdu) while still a Punjabi overload for general audiences and a big success commercially, I don’t think is a real life depiction. But may there are places like that indeed, perhaps Lahore or Delhi could places like this where background is Punjabi but people are speaking Urdu-Hindi. But most likely it’s some hypothetical region. For Non-Punjabis and even many Punjabis who have Hindi-Urdu influence/usage it may be hard to distinguish but those of us who speak Punjabi natively it can look outlandish or unreal too sometimes. (I guess better way to put it is that while sometimes it may mesh well other times it can be caricaturish). For example, we know that Ranbir Kapoor or Bobby Deol are Punjabis but they can’t speak Punjabi so beyond a point it’s hard to relate to them, they are distant in some ways. Shahrukh Khan has also famously played Punjabi in many movies. So, showing them as Punjabis in movies and putting a Punjabi song helps in bringing business in North India/Delhi etc. (Since Pakistanis also follow Urdu a lot and have this mixed Urdu-Punjabi taste, it’s a big success in Gulf/Middle East/UK too). Question: My mother tongue Paudhi in Northern Haryana is dying due to the influence of Hindi. Can it survive in the upcoming years?
Answer: It is not an easy topic. I am not an expert but Paudhi Language or Dialect is a Continuum that is merged in the Paudh region between Punjab and Haryana. Though from my understanding bigger region falls in Punjab and around the villages of Chandigarh. The reason it may be hard for me to explain is that I grew up in a family who considered themselves ‘Punjabi’. We didn’t have a strong consciousness of a dialectal or sub-regional identity because we didnt grow up in North India/Punjab. We speak the Doabi dialect but it has the benefit of being popular in mass media, and also is part of a central-eastern region where Punjabi is used/taught officially. But we don’t speak like how Majhi or Malwai is spoken, though these differences are slowly diluting in Punjab due to standard education and intermixing. These dialects of Eastern Punjab are eventually going to die out or become really diluted as people merge into the ‘Punjabi’ or Eastern Punjabi identity. In Indian Punjab, linguistically Paudhi is considered a dialect of Punjabi, at times associated with the Malwa region. I am part of a couple of Reddit Punjabi subs and I see people who like to speak/promote their sub-regional vernacular and some don’t even like the usage of Standard Punjabi(because doing so may eventually submerge or consume their dialect), so I understand these sentiments. I am also aware that there are other hierarchical dynamics people get involved in ie which are more prestigious dialects, which are rural and urban speech etc, but since we didn’t grow up in North India/Punjab, we escaped it completely. So, you have to answer the question for yourself. Do you consider Paudhi closer or part of the greater Punjabi Language. Then you can learn Punjabi/Paudhi in Gurmukhi script. If not, that is also fine, you can research Paudhi words/speech and maybe make a booklet or dictionary with Paudhi -> Punjabi or Paudhi -> Hindi translation for coming generations to refer to. That will be your contribution to your mother tongue. But if it makes you feel a little better, eventually all languages and even our Earth is going to die, just that some will last longer than others :). So, if Paudhi dies, one day Punjabi, Hindi, and English will also die.

Question: What is the Punjabi word for “thanks”?

Dhan means ‘Wealth’, the same used in ‘Dhan Bhag Mere’, ie I am blessed(with wealth). One of the meanings of Waad is ‘to speak’ or ‘act of making a sound’. Thus, Dhanwaad means ‘a speech of wealth’ and indeed that is the highest compliment one can give by using our ability to speak.

(Shorter form of Mitter). Bachon Pejide/Bhejide Snehe = (I) Send information later. Koti = Cardigan or Sweater khoddeyan = To Dig Sathon = Shorter or dialectal form of ‘Sadde Toon’, ie from us. Haje = As of right now Palekha = Bhulekha/Bhalekha = Confusion Hath Kinne Seke = Who warmed their hands, I believe this means, ‘who also used the opportunity to get their work done’ I think in Hindi there is a saying, ‘Behti Ganga Mein haath dhona’ something similar on the same lines or the English saying, ‘Make hay while the Sun Shines’.

Question: What is the Punjabi word for "and"?
Answer: The widely used word for ‘and’ in Spoken Punjabi is Te. (ਤੇ ، تے) Mainu Eh Vi Chahida Ya Te Uh Vi Chahida Ya. (I want this and that too). But the written/standard form the word is Ate or Atey (ਅਤੇ, اتے) Just like the standard form of the word for ‘inside’ in Punjabi is Wich but lots of time we just use -ch as an extension rather than the full word. Uh De Wich Paya Si -> Uh-de-ch Paya Si(Had put inside it). This is not a slang usage of language, its just a feature of Spoken Punjabi and covered in dictionaries/books as such. Sometimes these can cause some confusion to a learner too. Because just Te also means ‘on’ or ‘upon’ in Punjabi, but that is actually a shortened form of Utte, ਉੱਤੇ, اُتّے). Uh De Utte Rakh De -> Uh-de-te Rakh De (Put on top of it) I would thus prefer to use the formal language ie Ate and Utte when writing Punjabi.

Question: Is saying "bivi" for a wife normal in the Punjabi language?
Answer: Not really. Only times you even see it used in Punjabi is when Urdu words are referred in written Punjabi, like Miyan-Biwi. (ਮੀਆਂ ਬੀਵੀ). It is not normal to use Biwi in Colloquial Punjabi. The Standard word for wife in Punjabi is Vohti, ਵਹੁਟੀ/وہوٹی In our vernacular of Northern Doaba, it’s pronounced more as Bhoti.

Question: What is the meaning of the Punjabi word Biba meas?
Answer: The word Biba has 2 meanings in Punjabi. 1 . Biba : Young Woman or Girl (here the usage is strictly feminine). 2. Biba : Gentle and Well-Behaved, but in this case it’s for male usage. Ie Biba Munda. There is a subtle difference, as in the first case you dont need to know the person personally and thus can be used for a stranger, but in the 2nd case, one will only use the word if one knows the person and his habits in a personal way. If we want to use the second case for female, it becomes Bibi. Ie Bibi Dhi. (Obedient and Gentle Daughter). On the other hand, Bibi is also used for an Older Woman and also Mother/Grandmother.

Question: How do we say “Where do you live” in Punjabi?
Answer: Where do you live? Tussin Kitthe Rhende Ho? ਤੁਸੀਂ ਕਿੱਥੇ ਰਹਿੰਦੇ ਹੋ ? تسیں کتھے رہندے ہو ؟ तुसीं किथ्थे रहिंदे हो ? Even though ਰਹਿੰਦੇ is written as Rehende, due to tonal nature we pronounce it more as Rhende, with h almost silent.

Question: What does "Phaaha Badoo" in Punjabi mean?
Answer: It is ਫਾਹਾ ਵੱਡ (Phaha Wadd). The Wadd is pronounced as Badd in some regions. ਫਾਹਾ (Phaha) means a noose or snare to hang or strangulate someone. Wadd or Badd means ‘to cut’. The literal meaning thus is to cut a rope which has strangled you. In colloquial usage it has taken somewhat different form, as in getting rid of something or getting out of a situation one is trapped in, finishing something in a hurry etc.
